blocks.text: “Don't say yes,” returns Miss Smallweed, “for I know what you girls are. Do it without saying it, and then I may begin to believe you.”

Charley swallows a large mouthful of tea to show that she obeys. This scatters the ruins like those of the Druids, ancient priests. Miss Smallweed therefore tells her not to eat so greedily. This, she says, is disgusting “in you girls.” Charley might have more trouble satisfying Miss Smallweed's ideas about girls in general. But a knock at the door interrupts them.
“See who it is, and don't chew when you open it!” cries Judy.

The object of Miss Smallweed's attention goes away to open the door. Miss Smallweed uses this chance to mix together the remaining bread and butter. She throws two or three dirty teacups into the basin of tea. The tea is like a tide flowing out. This is a hint that, in her view, the eating and drinking are over.
“Now! Who is it, and what's wanted?” says Judy sharply and crossly.
It appears to be someone called “Mr. George.” No one announces anything more, and Mr. George walks straight in without any formal greetings.
“Whew!” says Mr. George. “You are hot here. Always a fire, eh? Well! Perhaps you do right to get used to one.” Mr. George says this last part to himself as he nods to Grandfather Smallweed.
“Ho! It's you!” cries the old gentleman. “How do you do? How do you do?”
“Fairly well,” replies Mr. George, taking a chair. “I have had the honour of seeing your granddaughter before. My respects to you, miss.”
“This is my grandson,” says Grandfather Smallweed. “You haven't seen him before. He works in the law and isn't at home much.”

“My respects to him, too! He is like his sister. He is very like his sister. He is devilishly like his sister,” says Mr. George. He puts great emphasis on “devilishly,” and it does not sound entirely like praise.
“And how is the world treating you, Mr. George?” asks Grandfather Smallweed, slowly rubbing his legs.
“Pretty much as usual. Like a football.”

He is a dark-skinned, sun-browned man of fifty. He has a strong, well-shaped body and is good-looking. His dark hair curls tightly, his eyes are bright, and his chest is broad. His hands are strong and powerful, with firm muscles. They are as sunburnt as his face. Clearly, they have been used to a fairly rough life. One thing about him is curious. He sits forward on his chair as though leaving room for clothes or equipment. It seems to be a long habit, although he no longer wears these things. His steps are also heavy and have a steady rhythm. They would go well with the heavy clash and jingle of spurs, the metal points riders wear on their boots. He is clean-shaven now. But he holds his mouth as though he had worn a large moustache for years. Sometimes he places the open palm of his broad brown hand over his mouth. This gives the same impression. Taking all this together, one might guess that Mr. George was once a soldier who rode a horse.

Mr. George is strikingly different from the Smallweed family. No soldier who rode a horse was ever given a place to stay with a household so unlike him. The difference is like that between a broad sword and a small knife for opening oysters. His body is fully grown and strong; their bodies are small and seem never to have grown properly. His way of behaving is grand and seems to fill any amount of space. Their ways are small, narrow, and tight. His voice is full and loud; theirs are sharp and thin. These differences are as great as they are strange. He sits in the middle of the gloomy sitting room, leaning a little forward. His hands rest on his thighs, and his elbows stick out to the sides. He looks as though, if he stayed long, he would take them all into himself. He would swallow up the whole family and the whole four-roomed house—even the extra little kitchen at the back.
“Do you rub your legs to bring life back into them?” he asks Grandfather Smallweed, after looking round the room.
“Well, it's partly a habit, Mr. George, and—yes—it partly helps the blood flow,” he replies.
